Hearing that Kokoro “helped you realize” this dream makes her see you as a kind of big‑brother hero, and it makes her want to cheer both of you on by enjoying the enchiladas as enthusiastically as possible. Right now she just wants to be your most energetic assistant—fetching, tasting, and hyping you up—so that cooking for them can feel as special for you as it sounds like it was with Kokoro.

The scent of browning beef deepens, fat popping softly as you work the wooden spatula through it. The little kitchen cocoon of light and sound makes the rest of the apartment feel further away than it is.

“Yes, I really loved Kokoro very much. You know…” Your voice lifts, brightening along with your expression. “If I did not go into math, I am sure I would have become a chef. There is something magical about cooking food and seeing someone else enjoy it. And we live in a global economy; we have any ingredient from any part of the world at our disposal. I think Kokoro helped me realize that.”

You say it with your hands as much as with your mouth—one lifting from the spatula to sketch an invisible globe in the air, fingers splaying as if you can almost pluck spices straight out of the sky and drop them into the pan. The earlier shadow around her name thins under this new light; for a moment, you’re not the bumbling “professor” but someone younger, eyes lit up by the idea of saffron from here, chilies from there, melted together into something that makes another person’s face light up.

Miku, slicing the last onion into even arcs, slows to listen. The word “magical” makes the corners of her lips twitch, like she’s not sure if she’s allowed to believe it. “Becoming a… chef,” she repeats softly, as if trying the idea of you in a different life on for size. She imagines you and this invisible Kokoro at another countertop, another cutting board, and something tender and a little painful stirs. Her knife work, though, stays precise; if anything, she’s more careful now, as if not wasting a single slice is part of honoring whatever you and Kokoro discovered in some other kitchen.

Itsuki’s hands are busy arranging spices, but your little monologue about a “global economy” and “ingredients from any part of the world” makes her pause mid‑reach. It doesn’t sound like your usual puffed‑up act; there’s a quiet conviction in it that sits differently. “…Cooking ‘magically’ doesn’t exempt you from proper nutrition and technique,” she says, almost reflexively, but the usual bite is dulled. Her eyes skim the neatly chopped onions, the well‑browned meat, then flick to your animated profile. “Still… if you really considered becoming a chef, that would explain why you seem so at ease here.” The admission is wary, but it’s an admission.

At your side, Yotsuba is rapt, elbows planted on the counter, chin in her hands as she watches you conjure pictures of far‑off ingredients. “Wow… a global economy of enchiladas,” she breathes, utterly sincere. “Kokoro must’ve been so happy, getting to taste all your experiments.” The thought delights her so much she bounces once on her heels. “If you ever *do* become a chef, I’ll totally be your number‑one taste‑tester! I’ll order the extra‑spicy Kokoro Special every time!” The promise is half joke, half oath.

From the doorway, Nino’s eyes narrow, not at the cooking but at the way your whole face changes when you talk like this. The specificness—“global economy,” “ingredients from any part of the world,” “Kokoro helped me realize that”—lands too cleanly to dismiss as random fluff, and that annoys her more than obvious lies would. “You sure like spinning pretty speeches,” she says, arms still crossed. “Almost sounds real when you say it like that.” Her gaze slides over the pan, to your easy posture at their stove. “If this is another performance, you’re really going all‑in, huh.”

Ichika watches the exchange in profile, her head tipped just so. Your brightened expression, the way the word “magical” softens your eyes, the idea of a path‑not‑taken chef version of you traced out by Kokoro’s tastes—they all slot in alongside the lines she saw in your notebook: Yotsuba: very smart! and, below that, For Kokoro. “A magical, globe‑trotting chef who almost was,” she muses lightly, pushing off the counter
